lesson_title: A Torch, a Wall and the Whole Planet's Weather
hook_text: The sun shines just as hard on Antarctica as on Musina. So why is one a freezer?
clip_script: Shine a torch straight at a wall and you get a small, tight, blazing circle. Now tilt it. Same torch, same battery, same light — but it spreads into a big, stretched, dim oval. Nothing was lost. It was just shared over more wall. That is the entire equator-and-poles story. The sun shines equally on all of us, but near the equator the beam hits almost straight on and lands in a small hot circle, while the earth's curve turns the poles sideways and the same beam smears into a weak oval. And the poles get punished twice, because slanting light must push through way more air — like cutting diagonally across a packed taxi rank instead of walking straight over. It arrives spread thin and already robbed. Then colour finishes the job: ice and snow are the whitest surfaces on earth and bounce the sunlight straight back, while the dark ocean is the black bakkie in the parking lot, soaking up nearly everything. Hot circle, dim oval, white bounce, dark soak. That is why the tropics have too much energy and the poles never have enough — and why every wind and every ocean current on this planet is basically a delivery vehicle carrying the difference.
visual_style: A torch beam on a dark wall morphing into sunlight on a rotating globe; the bright circle at the equator and the smeared oval at the pole labelled in real time; a split shot of a white bakkie and a black bakkie baking in a Karoo car park.
mood: Curious and clarifying, building to planetary scale.
pacing: Slow reveal on the torch tilt, quick beats for path length and albedo, wide expansive close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and work out any place's midday sun height for any date.
